site.name: LoseWeight.net
site.tagline: Calculate a realistic, evidence-based path to your goal weight.
site.description: Free calculators and evidence-based guides with transparent sourcing and review status. Get a realistic timeline, calorie range, and weekly milestones for your goal weight.

home.trustBody: Calculators run in your browser and no measurement reaches our servers. Guides cite primary sources next to the claims they support, and each one states plainly whether a clinician has reviewed it. Where evidence is uncertain, the page says so.
home.quickTitle: How long will it take, realistically?
home.quickLead: Five fields. You get a calorie range, a date, and the week-by-week curve behind it. Nothing is sent to us.
home.quickResultLead: At this pace you would reach {goal} around
home.quickNaive: A fixed-rate calculator would have said {weeks} weeks. It ignores that a lighter body burns less.
home.quickNotReached: On this intake, weight flattens out around {weight} before reaching your goal.
home.quickGoalHigh: Set a goal below your current weight to see a plan.
home.reason1: Your maintenance falls as you get lighter, so the same intake produces a smaller deficit over time. The curve bends. A fixed rate cannot show that.
home.reason2: Expenditure drops a little further than body-composition change alone predicts. This model includes that effect and caps it, rather than ignoring it or exaggerating it into a reason nothing works.
home.reason3Title: It shows a range, not a promise
home.reason3: Predictive equations are estimates, not measurements, and they miss by more for some people than others. The plan says so, and shows you how to correct it from three weeks of your own weigh-ins.
home.loopBody: The plan is a starting hypothesis. The tracker records what actually happens, compares it against the projection, and the plateau analyzer reads the same data to tell you whether a flat week means anything yet.
home.loopStep1: Build a plan and save it to this browser.
home.loopStep2: Weigh in and read the 7 day average, not the daily number.
home.loopStep3: After three weeks, compare the trend against the plan and adjust once.
home.source1: Hall KD, Chow CC. Why is the 3500 kcal per pound weight loss rule wrong? International Journal of Obesity, 2013.
home.source2: Rosenbaum M, Leibel RL. Adaptive thermogenesis in humans. International Journal of Obesity, 2010.
home.source3: Mifflin MD et al. A new predictive equation for resting energy expenditure in healthy individuals. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 1990.

planner.title: Weight loss planner
planner.intro: Fill in five fields. You get a calorie target, a realistic date, and the week-by-week curve behind it.
planner.sexNote: Used only by the metabolic rate equation, which has separate versions for male and female bodies. If these differ for you, the male version generally fits a higher lean mass.
planner.chartNote: The straight line is what a fixed-rate calculator would tell you. The curve accounts for the fact that a lighter body burns less.
planner.milestoneHealthy: Top of the healthy BMI range
planner.goalTooLow: That goal is below the healthy BMI range for your height ({min}). Consider setting a goal inside the range, or talk to a clinician first.
planner.goalAboveCurrent: Your goal weight is above your current weight. This planner is built for weight loss.
planner.clampedFloor: Your requested rate would put you below {floor} calories a day, which is the lowest we will suggest without medical supervision. The plan uses {floor} instead, so it will take longer than the rate you picked.
planner.clampedDeficit: Your requested rate needs a deficit larger than 25% of your maintenance. Larger deficits cost more lean tissue and are harder to sustain, so the plan uses a 25% deficit instead.
planner.plateauNote: On this intake, weight loss flattens out around {weight} before reaching your goal. To go further you would need to lower intake again or add activity, and recalculate at that point.
planner.assumptions: Predictive equations carry real error. Your actual maintenance may sit 10 to 15% either side of the estimate. Treat the number as week one's experiment: track your weight for three weeks, compare the trend against the projection, then adjust by 100 to 200 calories.
planner.savedNote: Saved in this browser only. There is no account and no sync.
planner.saveFailed: Could not save. Your browser may be blocking storage or out of space.
planner.firstWeekIntro: These three weeks are for measuring, not for pushing. Set the four numbers below, keep everything else as it already is, and let the trend tell you whether the estimate was right for you.
planner.fwDontChange: Do not adjust the calorie target before {date}, whatever the scale does in week one. Early swings are water, not fat, and reacting to them is what makes a plan unreadable.
planner.scenarioGentleTradeoff: Easiest to live with and the kindest to muscle. Slow enough that a distant goal may level off before you reach it.
planner.scenarioStandardTradeoff: The usual middle. Fast enough to stay motivating, slow enough to survive a bad week.
planner.scenarioFasterTradeoff: As fast as is sensible. More hunger, more lean tissue lost, and the hardest to hold when life interferes.
planner.scenarioNotFor: Less suitable if you train hard, are already lean, or have a history of restrictive eating.
planner.rangeNote: Shown as a range because the underlying equation is an estimate, not a measurement.
planner.rateSuggested: Around {rate} a week suits your starting point.
planner.scenarioReaches: Levels off around {weight}, short of your goal
planner.scenarioMilestone: 10% of body weight in about {weeks} weeks
planner.scenarioAllSafe: All three sit inside safe limits for your numbers. The fastest is capped at a 25% deficit, or the lowest intake we will suggest without medical supervision, whichever comes first.
planner.fwMovementValue: Keep your usual activity. Changing it now makes the calorie estimate impossible to check.
planner.routineTitle: Turn this into a weekly plan
planner.routineBody: The target above is a number. Tell us how you normally eat and we will pick three changes that get you there, built from the food you already have.

tracker.title: Progress tracker
tracker.intro: Log your weight and read the 7 day average, not the daily number. Day to day swings of 1 to 2 kg come from water, food in transit, and sodium, and they are larger than a week of real fat loss.
tracker.noEntries: No weigh-ins yet. Add your first one to start the trend line.
tracker.localOnly: Your weigh-ins are saved in this browser only. Clearing site data or switching device loses them, so export a backup now and then.
tracker.needThreeWeeks: Add three weeks of weigh-ins to get a reliable read on your rate.
tracker.plateauNone: Your 7 day average is still moving down. Nothing to fix.
tracker.plateauShort: Your average has been flat for {weeks} weeks. That is still within normal fluctuation. A plateau needs three or more flat weeks before it means anything.
tracker.plateauReal: Your average has been flat for {weeks} weeks. That qualifies as a plateau. The usual cause is that your maintenance fell as you lost weight, so recalculate your plan at your current weight before cutting calories further.
tracker.backupHint: There is no account and no cloud sync. The export file is your backup.
tracker.noPlan: You have not saved a plan yet.
tracker.importEmpty: No usable rows found in that file.
tracker.chartSummary: Weight trend from {start} to {end}. Started at {startWeight}, latest 7 day average {latest}, change {change}.
tracker.invalidWeight: Enter a weight between 20 and 500 kg.
tracker.invalidDate: Pick a date that is not in the future.

calculators.title: Calculators
calculators.intro: Each calculator runs in your browser and shows the formula it used.
calculators.tdeeDesc: What your body burns in a day, broken into resting rate and movement.
calculators.bmiDesc: Your BMI, what the category means, and the weight range it maps to at your height.
calculators.whtrDesc: A better predictor of individual risk than BMI, and it needs only a tape measure.
calculators.proteinDesc: How much protein protects lean mass in a deficit, and how much fiber fits your intake.
calculators.plateauDesc: Check whether a stall is a real plateau or normal fluctuation, and what to change first.
calculators.waistHelp: Measure at the midpoint between your lowest rib and the top of your hip bone, at the end of a normal breath out. Keep the tape snug without compressing the skin.
calculators.bodyFatHelp: If you know it from a DEXA scan, the calculator uses the Katch-McArdle equation instead, which is more accurate.
calculators.weeksFlat: Weeks with no change in your 7 day average
calculators.plateauNeedsData: This reads the weigh-ins you have saved in the tracker on this device. Add a few weeks of entries and come back.
calculators.vInsufficientWhy: You have {days} days of weigh-ins. Three weeks is the minimum before a flat stretch means anything, because daily swings are larger than a week of fat loss.
calculators.vSparse: Too few weigh-ins to read a trend
calculators.vSparseWhy: You are averaging {perWeek} weigh-ins a week over {days} days. A 7 day average needs at least three or four readings a week to be stable. Weigh more often before drawing conclusions.
calculators.vOnTrackWhy: Your 7 day average is falling at about {rate} a week. Nothing needs changing.
calculators.vNormalWhy: Your average has been flat for {weeks} week or so. That is inside normal water and gut-content variation. Wait until you have three or more flat weeks.
calculators.vSlowerWhy: You are losing about {rate} a week against a plan of {planned}. That is still progress, so the first thing to check is measurement, not calories.
calculators.vPlateauWhy: Your average has not moved for {weeks} weeks with consistent weighing. The usual cause is that your maintenance fell as you lost weight.
calculators.stepData: Confirm the data first. Weigh daily under the same conditions and read only the 7 day average.
calculators.stepMeasure: Weigh your food for one week instead of estimating. Reported intake drifts upward over months and you cannot see it from the inside.
calculators.stepActivity: Check whether your daily movement has dropped. It usually does in a deficit, without you deciding to.
calculators.stepRecalc: Recalculate your energy needs at your current weight, not your starting weight. For you that is about {maintenance} calories.
calculators.stepAdjust: Only then consider 100 to 150 fewer calories, and give it two weeks.
calculators.stepProfessional: If the stall persists past that, or you are losing hair, sleeping badly, or your period has stopped, speak to a clinician rather than cutting further.
calculators.contextHint: These do not change the numbers. They change how much confidence to put in them.
calculators.ctxCycle: I menstruate and could be in the second half of my cycle
calculators.ctxIllness: Recent illness, travel, or a big change in routine
calculators.ctxSodium: Noticeably saltier food than usual in the last few days
calculators.ctxTraining: Started or increased resistance training recently
calculators.ctxNote: Water retention from any of these can hide two to three weeks of real fat loss. It is worth waiting another two weeks before changing anything.

guides.title: Guides
guides.intro: Written to answer the question you came with. Sources are attached to the claims they support.
guides.notReviewed: This guide is written by {name} but has not yet completed his medical accuracy review. It is based on the sources listed at the end. Check anything affecting your treatment with your own doctor.
guides.empty: No guides have been published in this language yet.
guides.emptyNote: Guides on LoseWeight.net are written separately for each language rather than machine translated, so a guide written in another language will not appear here.
guides.reviewedSelf: Written and reviewed for medical accuracy by {name}, a physician educated at Azerbaijan Medical University with a professional background in pediatrics in Azerbaijan. He is not licensed to practice medicine in the United States.

newsletter.title: Get the practical stuff
newsletter.body: One email when a new guide or calculator goes up. No daily motivation, no selling.
newsletter.success: You're on the list. We'll email you when a new guide or calculator goes up.
newsletter.error: That didn't work. Try again in a moment.
newsletter.label: Email address
newsletter.privacy: We store your address and the page you subscribed from, nothing else. One email per new guide or calculator, unsubscribe in any of them.
newsletter.noConfirm: No confirmation email is sent yet, because sending is not set up. You are on the list.

footer.disclaimer: LoseWeight.net provides general health information and calculators. It does not provide medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment, and it is not a substitute for a licensed clinician who knows your history.

common.notFoundBody: The page you asked for does not exist, or it was published in a different language.

activity.lightDesc: Light exercise 1 to 3 days a week
activity.moderateDesc: Moderate exercise 3 to 5 days a week
activity.activeDesc: Hard exercise 6 to 7 days a week
activity.athleteDesc: Physical job or training twice a day

authors.reviewNote: Because the author and the reviewer are the same person, articles here say "written and reviewed for medical accuracy" rather than "independently reviewed". Independent review by a second clinician is not currently part of the process, and pages say so.
authors.noArticles: No published articles in this language yet.
authors.pediatrics: Trained and worked as a pediatrician in Azerbaijan

onboarding.title: How do you normally eat?
onboarding.intro: Describe a typical day in your own words. One paragraph is enough. We turn it into a list you can correct before anything is calculated.
onboarding.placeholder: Breakfast is usually toast and coffee. Lunch is whatever is at work, often chicken and rice. Dinner varies. I snack in the afternoon and I will not give up my evening tea.
onboarding.consentBody: To read this properly we send the text you write above, and nothing else, to an AI provider. Your name, email and weigh-ins are not included, and we do not allow it to be used for training. We keep the structured result, not the raw text.
onboarding.consentAccept: Send the text to be interpreted
onboarding.consentDecline: Do not send it. Read it on this device, where nothing leaves your browser. Writing one meal per line helps it read you accurately.
onboarding.reviewIntro: Nothing has been calculated yet. Correct anything wrong, then continue.
onboarding.noMatchHelp: Rename it to something more common, or leave it out. We will not guess a value for it.
onboarding.portionUnknown: Portion not stated, so we assumed a typical one
onboarding.mixedDish: A mixed dish, so this is a range rather than a number
onboarding.markNonNegotiable: Mark as something you will not give up
onboarding.estimatedNote: A range, because portions and mixed dishes are estimates. This is a starting point to test against your own weigh-ins.
onboarding.nothingParsed: We could not read a routine from that. Try describing your meals one per line.
onboarding.refused: That looks like a medical question. This tool plans food and habits, and cannot answer it.
onboarding.refusedUrgent: If this is a medical emergency, contact your local emergency number rather than this site.
onboarding.someUncertain: Plus {count} where the portion or dish is an estimate, which is normal and does not need fixing.
onboarding.chooseMatchHelp: Pick the closest one. Until you do, it counts as nothing.
onboarding.portionFromWords: Worked out from how you described it, so it is approximate
onboarding.recipeProposed: We assumed what is in this
onboarding.recipeIntro: No database has a figure for this dish, so we priced what is usually in it. Check it, because the amounts vary by household.
onboarding.recipeMissing: We found no data for {items}, so the total is lower than the real one.

fat.title: Measure the {food} instead of pouring it
fat.rationale: Cooking fat is the cheapest calorie to cut, because it changes how much you eat, not what you eat. A tablespoon poured by eye is often two. Measuring the same dish saves about {saved} kcal a day and tastes the same.

alt.spray: Use a spray oil for frying
alt.measure: Measure with a spoon, do not pour
alt.nonstick: Use a nonstick pan and less fat

liquid.title: Replace the {food} you drink
liquid.rationale: Drinks with calories do not make you feel full, so they add to the day rather than replacing part of it. This one is about {saved} kcal. Swapping it changes nothing about your meals.

protein.title: Add about {grams} g of protein at {meal}
protein.rationale: You are eating less, so hunger is the thing most likely to end this. Protein is the part of a meal that keeps you full longest. This adds food rather than removing it, so it saves no calories by itself.

fiber.title: Add about {grams} g more fiber
fiber.rationale: Fiber fills you up and helps with the digestion changes that often come with eating less. It is also where most people fall short. Like protein, this adds food and saves nothing on its own.

alt.beans: A portion of beans or lentils

portion.title: Take about {percent}% less {food}
portion.rationale: You keep the food. Cutting a quarter of the largest portion is usually not noticed after a week, and here it is worth roughly {saved} kcal a day. We would rather shrink a portion than ban a food you like.

alt.serveless: Serve less, go back only if still hungry
alt.halfnow: Put half away before you start

snack.title: Plan something to eat when you are hungriest
snack.rationale: You said {when} is when hunger hits. An unplanned hungry moment is where most days come apart, so it is worth deciding now rather than at the time. This is not about cutting calories.

alt.fruitnuts: Fruit and a small handful of nuts

cooking.title: Cook once, eat twice
cooking.rationale: You said you rarely cook, which usually means more meals decided while hungry. Cooking a double portion once removes that decision on the second day and typically saves 100 to 250 kcal, because the alternative is whatever is nearest.

alt.assembly: Keep ingredients that need no cooking

unknown.order: If you eat out, decide what you want before hunger makes the decision for you.
unknown.drink: Water is the simplest default with a restaurant meal. Choose another drink when you actually want it.
unknown.portion: Restaurant portions vary. Stop when you are comfortably full and take the rest with you if that is practical.

often.order: Decide what you are having before you look at the menu. Ordering hungry is how the plan goes sideways.
often.drink: Drink water with the meal. Restaurant drinks are often a third of the calories and none of the fullness.
often.half: Ask for half to be boxed at the start, or move it aside before you begin.

rare.enjoy: You eat out rarely, so eat what you actually want. One meal does not undo a week.
rare.drink: If you want a drink, have it instead of dessert rather than as well as.
rare.next: Go back to normal at the next meal, not tomorrow. There is nothing to make up for.

hunger.unknown: You have not selected a usual hungry time, so keep one practical option available rather than assuming when hunger will arrive.
hunger.morning: You are hungriest in the morning, so put most of your protein at breakfast rather than saving it for later.
hunger.afternoon: Your hunger comes in the afternoon. Have something ready by mid-morning, because deciding at 4pm rarely goes well.
hunger.evening: Evening is your hard part. Keep more of the day's food for the evening rather than eating light and fighting it later.
hunger.late-night: Late night is when it slips. Decide before dinner whether you are eating again, and what.
hunger.varies: Your hunger is not on a schedule, so keep one planned option available all day rather than timing it.
hunger.protein: When you are hungry between meals, eat protein first. It works better than a small sweet thing that leaves you looking for another.
hunger.wait: If you are unsure whether it is hunger, have a glass of water and wait ten minutes. Sometimes it is, and then you eat.

situation.flexible: One meal a week is yours, unplanned and uncounted. It is part of the plan, not a break from it.

weekly.title: Three changes, built from what you already eat
weekly.intro: Nothing here removes a food you said you will not give up. Reject anything that does not fit your week.
weekly.keepBody: {count} of your foods are untouched. That is the point: a plan you can follow is one that still looks like your week.
weekly.worth: Worth about {low} to {high} kcal a day
weekly.worthNothing: Saves nothing by itself, and that is deliberate
weekly.totalWeekly: Around {low} to {high} kg a week, if you follow it
weekly.totalCaveat: This is energy balance arithmetic, not a promise. Real weight moves with water and glycogen too, especially in the first fortnight. Your own weigh-ins will correct this within three weeks.
weekly.shortOfTarget: These changes do not reach your calorie target on their own. That is better than stacking more changes than anyone keeps up. We will adjust from your actual weigh-ins rather than guessing harder now.
weekly.noneAccepted: You have rejected every change. Put at least one back, or start again with a different routine.
weekly.noPlan: Set a calorie target first, then come back. The changes are chosen to close the gap between what you eat now and that target.
weekly.noRoutine: Describe how you normally eat first.
weekly.savedBody: Three changes, everything else unchanged. From here the useful page is today, which shows only what this day asks of you.
weekly.noSaving: What you described already lands near your calorie target, so nothing here cuts calories.
weekly.noSavingWhy: That is worth treating with suspicion rather than satisfaction. Estimating a day of eating from a description is rough, and most people under-describe by more than they expect, usually the oil, the drinks and the second helpings. The changes above are about hunger and habit, which is what makes the next three weeks survivable. Your weigh-ins will settle the arithmetic better than any guess we can make now.

today.title: Today
today.eatIntro: Your own foods, not a menu. Pick whichever fits the day.
today.streak: Followed on {done} of the last {total} days
today.noPlan: You have not started a week yet.
today.noJudgement: A missed day is data, not a failure. The plan adjusts from what actually happens.

review.title: How the plan is going
review.maintenance: This is a maintenance week. Your actions and consistency still count, but weight-loss speed is not being judged and stable weight is not a stall.
review.tooEarly: It is day {days}. Weight moves with water, salt and glycogen by more than a week of real fat loss, so nothing here is worth reading yet. We do not adjust before day {min}, and neither should you.
review.notEnoughData: You have {weighIns} weigh-ins since starting. A trend needs at least four to mean anything. Weigh yourself a few more times, ideally at the same time of day.
review.notFollowing: You followed the full plan on {percent}% of the days you answered. That is not a criticism, it is a reason not to change the numbers: making a plan you are not following harder will not help. Worth asking which of the three is the one getting in the way.
review.onTrack: You are losing about {actual} kg a week, against roughly {expected} planned. That is close enough that the difference is measurement, not meaning. Nothing needs changing.
review.faster: You are losing about {actual} kg a week, faster than the {expected} planned. That usually means eating well under target, which costs muscle and is hard to keep up. Easing off now is not losing ground.
review.slower: You are losing about {actual} kg a week, against {expected} planned. The gap works out to roughly {gap} kcal a day. One more change is the measured response, rather than cutting everything further.
review.noChange: Your weight has not moved in {days} days on a plan you did follow. That is worth asking a clinician about rather than cutting further, because thyroid problems, some medications and fluid retention all do this and none of them are fixed by eating less.

action.fix-adherence: Look at what is getting in the way

review.noPlan: Start a week first, then this page has something to compare against.
review.allDeferred: You answered every day and set every change aside, each time for a reason. That is worth taking at face value: the plan has not really been tested, so changing the numbers would be guesswork. The more useful question is which of the three keeps getting in the way, and whether a different one would fit your week better.
